clue.text: Friend kept back after school scripture lesson: it increases pressure

indicators.note: keeping something back holds it behind, so the name is set down back to front
coming after places this piece at the end, following the earlier ones in sequence

blocks.note: RE is Religious Education, the school subject
Ross is one of the six characters in the sitcom Friends

explanation.surface: A pal is held back after a school RE lesson, and the whole episode is stressful.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital F is the tip: Friend means a character from the TV show Friends. COMP is the everyday British name for a comprehensive (state secondary) school.
explanation.definitionFit: A compressor is a machine that squeezes gas or air into a smaller volume, raising the pressure inside.

clue.text: Island copper gets qualification

blocks.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

explanation.surface: A policeman on an island earns a qualification.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' invites a police officer, but here it is the metal and its chemical symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: Cuba is the large Caribbean nation lying south of Florida, a single main landmass surrounded by sea.

clue.text: Jaws was back, with Bond’s boss replacing head of Spectre

indicators.note: going back runs the word in the opposite direction, from its end to its start
the head is the top or front, so just the opening letter
to replace is to take one letter's place, so one letter swaps in for another

blocks.note: taken as written, then turned round
M is James Bond's chief at MI6
the first letter of the word, which is swapped out

explanation.surface: A Bond-film scene: the henchman Jaws returns, and M takes over from the head of the villains' organisation SPECTRE.
explanation.walkthrough: Jaws is a Bond villain, so the whole clue feels like film trivia. Reverse 'was' to SAW, then M replaces its first letter S.
explanation.definitionFit: A maw is the mouth or gullet of a greedy animal, so it is a fair synonym for an animal's gaping mouthparts.

clue.text: Examination in Art is erroneously withdrawn

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the words that follow, spanning their word breaks
withdrawing pulls something back, so the concealed letters read backwards

blocks.note: the run of letters across the word breaks, before turning round

explanation.surface: An art exam paper is pulled because of a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Erroneously' looks like an anagram signal, but it simply supplies letters for the concealed string arT IS ERroneously, read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A resit is a second attempt at a test after failing it the first time, so it is one kind of examination.

clue.text: Poet’s old love choked by nerve gas

indicators.note: something choked is gripped tightly all round, so it ends up enclosed

blocks.note: sass is cheek or impudence, like nerve
N is the symbol for nitrogen, a gas

explanation.surface: A poet's former sweetheart is killed by a nerve agent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nerve gas' reads as one weapon, but it is two pieces, cheek plus nitrogen, and the 's stands for 'is'. Siegfried Sassoon was an English First World War poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Siegfried Sassoon wrote famous war poetry from the trenches of 1914 to 1918.

clue.text: Creature arisen, upset after prince cracks eggs

indicators.note: breaking into something puts a piece inside its shell
in a down entry, rising means reading from the bottom upwards
placed after means it comes at the end of the sequence

blocks.note: to muss is to mess up or dishevel

explanation.surface: A monster has risen, angry, after a prince breaks some eggs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arisen, upset' sounds like a riled beast; really MUSS (upset) is turned upward, and the prince sits between two egg-shaped Os.
explanation.definitionFit: The opossum is an American marsupial mammal, so it is an example of an animal.

clue.text: Substitute rejected pads

indicators.note: a rejected thing is sent back, so the word goes back to front

blocks.note: pads are the soft paws of an animal

explanation.surface: Replacement pads have been turned down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pads' suggests cushions or notepads; it means animal feet.
explanation.definitionFit: To substitute one thing for another is to exchange them, the verb sense of this word.

clue.text: Where in Lancashire fans make such a noise?

indicators.note: names a regional accent, so the word is said the way a local speaker would pronounce it

blocks.note: in a Lancashire accent the vowel is closer to 'wur'

explanation.surface: Asking where in Lancashire football supporters make such a racket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fans' suggests football crowds, but here they are electric fans. Lancashire is a county in north-west England known for its broad accent.
explanation.definitionFit: A whirr is the steady buzzing hum of spinning blades or machinery, the sound electric fans produce.

clue.text: Bullies ultimately keen to break media injunctions

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is used
breaking into something puts the piece inside it

blocks.note: the press is the news media
gagging orders are court injunctions stopping publication
the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: Tabloid bullies are itching to break court injunctions against the media.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as newspapers flouting gagging orders; the final letter of 'keen' breaks into GAGS.
explanation.definitionFit: To press-gang someone is to force or coerce them into doing something, which is bullying them.

clue.text: Troops run shelters to follow drug dealer

indicators.note: a shelter gives cover all round, so these letters go inside

blocks.note: to tail someone is to follow them

explanation.surface: Soldiers track down a drug dealer, hiding him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drug dealer' reads as one phrase, but the definition is just 'dealer'; 'drug' supplies ecstasy's letter. 'Troops run' together form the shell.
explanation.definitionFit: A retailer sells goods to the public, and a dealer is someone who trades in goods.

clue.text: Bishop playing slow sport with Jack

indicators.note: playing around with something rearranges it freely

explanation.surface: A clergyman plays a leisurely game alongside a friend called Jack.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack looks like a person's name; in the game it is the small white target ball.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawn bowls is played by rolling weighted balls towards a small white ball called the jack.

clue.text: See VIP opt to play high hat

indicators.note: playing with letters moves them freely into a different order

explanation.surface: Watch a celebrity choose to perform a high hi-hat on the drums.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High hat' could suggest a drum cymbal, but it is a tall top hat.
explanation.definitionFit: A stovepipe hat is a tall cylindrical silk hat, like the one Abraham Lincoln wore.

clue.text: With nothing to lose, goes to the dodgy parts of town

indicators.note: losing something means it drops out of the letters
something dodgy is unreliable or crooked, so the letters are not in their proper order

blocks.note: zero looks like the letter O; one O is removed

explanation.surface: Someone with nothing to lose heads to the rough neighbourhoods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dodgy' seems to describe the parts of town, but it is the anagram signal; take one O from 'goes to the' first.
explanation.definitionFit: Ghettoes are deprived districts of a city where a minority group lives in segregation.

clue.text: Devil's features shaved top to bottom

indicators.note: in a down entry the first letter is moved from the top to the foot

blocks.note: shorn means cut close, as fleece or hair

explanation.surface: The devil's face has been shaved from head to toe.
explanation.walkthrough: Move the S of SHORN from the top of the column to the bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: The Devil is traditionally pictured with a pair of horns sprouting from his head.

clue.text: Returning note following a case of ‘fair dos’

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the letters run the other way
a case is the outside, so only the outer letters are kept
following puts this piece after the others in sequence

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the word
the fifth note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: Someone sends back a note about a matter of 'fair dos', a fair share for all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fair dos' is British slang for 'fair enough', but here 'dos' means hairdos. 'Fair' only gives its outside letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An Afro is a rounded, bushy natural hairstyle, so it is one kind of hairdo, or do.

clue.text: Drive a taxi, reversing round church in drunken scenes

definitions.note: plural phrase for a singular noun that names an orgy of revelling

indicators.note: reversing runs everything so far backwards
going round something encloses it

explanation.surface: A cabbie backs round a church amid scenes of drunken revelry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drive a taxi' seems to be one action, but 'Drive' is a noun meaning energy or verve. The reversal covers all three pieces before the church goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: A bacchanale is a wild drunken revel, named after the rites of Bacchus, the Roman god of wine.

clue.text: A government called to answer a criminal charge

definitions.note: elliptical: the verb means to call someone to answer a charge, with 'called' doing double duty

indicators.note: to be called is to be spoken aloud, so the words are voiced

blocks.note: a reign is a period of rule by a monarch

explanation.surface: A government is summoned to court to answer a criminal charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A reign' and the answer sound the same; 'called' serves both as the sound signal and as part of the meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: To arraign someone is to bring them before a court to hear and plead to the indictment against them.

clue.text: Fake daughter removed from Sir Tom podcast

indicators.note: removing takes something out, so a letter disappears
to cast is to throw or mould, so the letters are thrown into a new shape

blocks.note: only the first three letters are fodder; the remainder is the signal to rearrange
the abbreviation for daughter, the letter removed

explanation.surface: A bogus daughter is edited out of Sir Tom's podcast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Podcast' is split: the D goes from 'pod', and 'cast' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An impostor pretends to be someone else to deceive others, so the person is a fake or fraud.

clue.text: Force girl to keep one tipsy

indicators.note: keeping something means holding it inside

explanation.surface: A girl is made to look after a drunken companion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Force' looks like a verb, but it is the noun: an armed body of people. Lit is slang for drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: A militia is a body of citizen soldiers, so it is a military force.

clue.text: Gets toupee in case of thinness

indicators.note: a case is the outside shell, so only the outer letters count
in places one piece inside another

blocks.note: a toupee is a small hairpiece

explanation.surface: A man buys a toupee because his hair is thinning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets' looks like 'acquires' in the surface; it means 'understands'. To twig is British informal for grasp.
explanation.definitionFit: To twig is informal British English for suddenly understanding something, just as you 'get' a joke.

clue.text: Trace of sewage found in abandoned septic tank

indicators.note: a trace is the smallest amount, so just the opening letter
abandoned means wild and unrestrained, so the letters are thrown loose

explanation.surface: A trace of sewage is discovered in a disused septic tank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abandoned septic tank' reads naturally, but 'abandoned' is the anagram signal and only 'tank' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: A cesspit is a pit or container collecting sewage and waste water, much like a septic tank.

clue.text: Jenny entertained by draws in Scottish cups

indicators.note: a guest who is entertained is held within the host's home

blocks.note: a tie is a drawn match
a jenny is a female donkey

explanation.surface: Jenny is involved in drawn games in Scottish football cup competitions.
explanation.walkthrough: Jenny looks like a woman's name, and 'cups' like trophies; a jenny is a female donkey and the cups are drinking vessels.
explanation.definitionFit: A tassie is a Scots word for a small drinking cup or goblet, as in Burns's poem.

clue.text: Strong desire with artist returning for sculpture

indicators.note: with here means containing, the one piece sitting inside the other
returning goes back the way it came, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: a word for longing, whose middle two letters are replaced

explanation.surface: An artist feels a strong urge to return to sculpture.
explanation.walkthrough: The artist is already sitting inside the word for strong desire; only turning him round is needed, a neat one-step change.
explanation.definitionFit: A carving is a figure or design cut from wood or stone, which is a form of sculpture.

clue.text: Side salad of eel has slice of cucumber on top

indicators.note: a salad is a mixture, so the letters are tossed together
a slice is a thin piece, so only a single letter is taken
in a down entry, on top means this piece comes first

explanation.surface: A side salad of eel topped with a slice of cucumber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Side salad' is a menu item, but 'Side' is a football team. Chelsea is a Premier League club in London.
explanation.definitionFit: In football a side is a team, and Chelsea Football Club is a well-known English example.

clue.text: A German bearing last of gifts for her?

definitions.note: a pronoun standing for a woman's name

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: A German man arrives carrying presents for his lady.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bearing' looks like 'carrying', but it is a compass direction. The question mark signals that 'her' stands for a female name.
explanation.definitionFit: Agnes is a traditional girl's name, so it is one example of a woman who could be called her.

clue.text: He follows Nick, losing task finally: a comfortable position

indicators.note: to lose something is to have it removed
finally points to the end letter, the one that goes
following puts this piece after the other

blocks.note: the last letter of the word, which is removed

explanation.surface: A man succeeds Nick after he fails to finish a job, landing a cushy post.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop the K from Nick, then add HE.
explanation.definitionFit: A niche is a role or situation that suits someone perfectly, where they feel at home and settled.

clue.text: Most graceful Soviet letters regularly focus with Putin

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every other letter is kept
a focus is a centre, so the middle letter is taken

blocks.note: the first, third, fifth letters and so on

explanation.surface: Elegant Soviet letters are regularly the focus for Putin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letters' is part of the fodder, not an instruction: take every other letter of 'Soviet letters', then the centre of Putin.
explanation.definitionFit: Svelte means slender and elegant, so the superlative describes whoever is the most graceful and slim.

clue.text: Brass instrument, large and cylindrical

explanation.surface: Describing a big brass instrument that is large and tube-shaped.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface lists three features of a tuba; only the last word defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Tubal means relating to or shaped like a tube, and a tube is a hollow cylinder.

clue.text: He died pinching a loaf

indicators.note: to pinch is to squeeze between fingers, so one piece is gripped by the other

explanation.surface: A man died stealing a loaf of bread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pinching' looks like theft, but it means holding. 'Loaf' is Cockney rhyming slang: loaf of bread = head.
explanation.definitionFit: In rhyming slang 'use your loaf' means use your brain, so loaf stands for the skull.

clue.text: Newsreader briefly struggles with little fish

indicators.note: cut short, so the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: a news anchor presents the bulletin

explanation.surface: A TV newsreader has trouble with some small fish.
explanation.walkthrough: Clip the R from ANCHOR, then add VIES.
explanation.definitionFit: Anchovies are small, slender, oily sea fish, often salted and packed in tins.

clue.text: Apathetic Labour's leader in bed

indicators.note: the leader is the one in front, so the first letter
in puts one piece inside the other

blocks.note: a bed is a base or foundation, as a bed of gravel

explanation.surface: The Labour Party leader lies listlessly in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bed' suggests sleeping, but it is a foundation. Labour is one of Britain's two main political parties.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone blasé is unimpressed and indifferent through over-familiarity, close to showing no interest.

clue.text: Mountain with friend pushing Penny to the bottom

indicators.note: pushing a letter shifts its position along the word
in a down entry the bottom is the foot of the column, where the letter lands

blocks.note: p is the abbreviation for a penny: this names the letter that moves, adding nothing new

explanation.surface: On a mountain, a friend shoves Penny down to the foot.
explanation.walkthrough: Penny looks like a name; it is the coin's abbreviation, moved from the top of PAL to the bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: An alp is a high mountain, especially one in Switzerland's Alpine range.

clue.text: Pitcher throwing last of balls from gutter

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter
throwing something away discards it

blocks.note: the final letter, which is removed
a gutter is a drain, like a sewer

explanation.surface: A baseball pitcher tosses the last ball straight into the gutter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pitcher' and 'balls' suggest baseball; the pitcher is actually a jug.
explanation.definitionFit: A ewer is a large jug with a wide mouth, once used for carrying washing water, so a type of pitcher.

clue.text: Tailless fish rolled in seed, nuts and cooked in breadcrumbs

indicators.note: without a tail, so the final letter is cut off
rolling something over turns it round end to end
in places one piece inside the other
nuts means crazy, so the letters go haywire

blocks.note: the pollack is a food fish of the cod family

explanation.surface: A recipe: a fish with its tail cut off, rolled in seeds and nuts and cooked in breadcrumbs.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a coating recipe, but 'rolled' turns POLLAC round and 'nuts' scrambles SEED around it.
explanation.definitionFit: Escalloped is a variant of scalloped: baked in a dish with a crumb topping or sauce.
